iously obtained from him we were about to inaugurate service to

responsible for anything that might befall us if we went on without
first getting the permission of the military chief at Chengtu. Wee
were afraid that some fool soldier at Chengtu might take a shot at
us if we started in to land so there was nothing to do but get busy
on the telegraph line and try to fix up everything with the author-
ities at Chengtu before going over there. We were unable to get all
factions straightened out until today (Wednesday) and then the visi-
bility turned out to be zero and as a result here we are at the air-
port waiting for a chance to leave. It is now late and I know that
we will not be able to go on until tomorrow morning. Therefore Bond
operations manager for China National Aviation Corp., Chief Pilot
Allison who is doing the flying on this trip, and our Chinese man-

ager at Chungking have gone back to the city and Mr.Chaplain Postal
Commissioner at Shanghai, who is on the trip with us, and I are stay-
ing at the airport over night. We hope to get away early tomorrow mor
ning, fly to Chengtu 175 miles by air ( two weeks by sedan chair) and
return here the same day. We would like to spend more time there but
I should be back in Shanghai as soon as possible and by returning
tomorrow I can catch the regular plane from Chungking to Hankow on
Friday and then connect with the regular plane out of Hankow for
Shanghai on Saturday.
We have had a marvelous trip so far. Left Shanghai Friday morn-
ing and flew above great white fleecy clouds all the way to Hankow.
The sun was shining brightly on the louds and through the holes in
the clouds we could look down another two or three thousand feet to
the rice fields below. At Hankow we were held up by bad weather all
day Saturday which we spent
, in the Hankow Country Club watching a
base ball game taking a swim and in the evening going to a picture
show (Washington Masquerade) and if you please playing 18 holes of
minature golf. The following morning, Sunday, we left Hankow and flew
westward along the Yangstze to Ichang where the gorges begin. We then
folløwed the cavern like Yangstze for more than a hundred miles, the
same route was taken by Father and Mother and Ralph in 1929 but it re
quired almost a week for them against an hour for us. I took along a
borrowed camera and got some good movies of the gorges, that is I took
some great shots if they turn out 0.K. Plan to have the films devel-
oped and send them to Debby with the request that she forward them to
Ralph if he is not at the Lake. We had the good fortune to catch up
with the regular plane of CNAC while in the gorges and I got some good
pictures of that ship in the air. It was the first time that two air-
planes ever went through the gorges together and the natives were so
impressed that they forgot to pull their boats up stream while we were
flying over head, but instead just stared up at us.

Chungking is a city of over one million people. It is built
on a steep hill and the streets are nothing but steps. We arrived at
the airport at which I am now writing on a typewritter of the air-
advisor to General liu a Frenchman, and went up to Chungking from here
on a boat which bellongs to the Standard 01l Co. We called on Admiral
Ho who has charge of the "Battleships" belonging to the Warlord and
then crossed the river to the section where all of the foreign resid-
ents live ( the foreign colony numbers about 30) There is no hotel at
Chungking. Our people always stay with the representative of the Stan-
dard Oil Co., but Mr. Chapelain and I went to the Postal Commissioners
house for the night. He is a Dane. He arranged for a chair for me and
told me just where to catch it, but by the time I got back across the
river it was almost dark. My chair was waiting for me. I got in and
the carriers started alon a narrow path up the mountain side. The
slope and hight was about the same as Shelving rocio At times we went
along the edge of cligis where the slightest slip would have meant
disaster. It was a new experience which is now after three days quite
the common thing to do but that first trip will remain with me for a
H--- of a long time. The house to which I was taken is a most facin-
ating place built in the Chinese style surrounded by a beautiful gar-
den • The inside was full of reallyfine things collected during the tax
twenty odd years of residence in China of two very nice and tremend-
ously interesting people Mr.and Mrs. Holm. They had a dinner party for
Mr. Chapelain and me that night. I was the only American present. There
were three Frenchmen, one Swiss, one English, two Germans, one Dutchman
one Chinese, one Russian and one Italian. They all spoke nothing but
English which was something of a break for me. The next night Monday
I spent with the Standard 0il man and his wife. Coming down the next
morning (it takes an hour to walk or be carried up to his place) we
walked right by an opium den and stopped at the door to take a look.
